newsitem.title: FRANCE: French ex-PM says Jospin plans jeopardise euro.
newsitem.headline: French ex-PM says Jospin plans jeopardise euro.

text.p: Former conservative prime minister Edouard Balladur said on Friday the new Socialist-led government's policies would jeopardise France's plans to join a single European currency by jacking up spending.

The new government reiterated that France was committed to the euro from 1999 after Prime Minister Lionel Jospin outlined plans including creation of 700,000 jobs and cuts in the working week to 35 hours in a keynote speech on Thursday.

French media gave Jospin good marks for honesty in trying to redeem campaign promises but said he had put off painful budget decisions until the autumn. Trades unions criticised Jospin for raising the minimum wage by only four percent.
Balladur, who was premier in 1993-95, said it was already clear the policies of Jospin's "Pink-Green-Red" coalition would increase budget spending by "a good 50 billion francs" ($8.6 billion) a year.

"I didn't hear...any talk of reducing public spending," Balladur told Europe 1 radio. "On the contrary, it is going to be raised. That's not the way to revive growth. It's the opposite of what needs to be done."
"France has a big interest in entering Europe and building the single currency," Balladur said.
"In the current state of things, if spending is raised, if our social system is rigidified still further, I don't see how we will be able to stick to our European ambitions," he said.
France needs to cut its deficit to three percent of gross domestic product (GDP) in 1997 to qualify for the euro from 1999. In 1996, it was 4.2 percent.
Employment Minister Martine Aubry, Jospin's number two, insisted there was no contradiction between Jospin's spending plans and his intention to bring France into the euro.
"The fiscal and social reform will indeed allow the country to stay on track" for the euro, she told RTL radio.
At the same time, she said France would stimulate consumption, help the weakest and the unemployed, and channel aid to companies such as in the building sector.
"Everything is urgent," said Aubry, the daughter of former European Commission president Jacques Delors. "But the most urgent thing is jobs."
French markets were little changed on Friday. The CAC stock index opened fractionally lower.
Jospin, who has said he will not impose extra austerity to qualify for the euro, said first signs were that public finances were "serious" and that a full audit would be ready in mid-July.

Blaming outgoing governments for gaping deficits is routine in France. Jospin's conservative predecessor Alain Juppe accused Balladur -- a member of the same Gaullist party -- in 1995 of leaving revenues in a "calamitous" state.
Balladur said a 1993 review showed that the deficit was 360 billion francs ($62 billion), far above the 160 billion ($27 billion) estimated by the outgoing Socialist-led government.
Jospin said that he would stick to all his campaign promises but said it would require "time and perseverance".

The message, endorsed by the National Assembly in a vote of confidence on Thursday night, was clearly meant to contrast with the late Socialist president Francois Mitterrand, who reversed course after two years, and with conservative President Jacques Chirac, who did so after just six months in office in 1995.

"Lionel Jospin is socialist and intelligent. Not really cynical," the conservative daily Le Figaro wrote in an editorial. "However, he will need a lot of skill to reconcile what cannot be reconciled."
Le Parisien said in a front page headline "Jospin announced what he promised" -- as if that were unusual in French politics.
